speaker: The Chairman
text: Head V, Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, our economy today is less about weathering cyclical volatility and more about navigating deep structural change in the global order.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Geopolitical fragmentation, industrial policy competition, supply chain reconfiguration, decarbonisation pressures and rapid technological disruption have fundamentally reshaped the landscape.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Recent volatility in global technology stocks also reminds us how quickly shifts in risk sentiment can transmit across financial markets, trade and investment flows.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is now further amplified by escalating tensions in the Middle East, which are already driving energy price volatility, safe haven flows and heightened uncertainty across global markets and can translate into higher inflation, tighter financial conditions and weaker global growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For a small and open economy like Singapore, these external forces will continue to shape our growth trajectory.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Both labour productivity and total factor productivity must become our primary engine of growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Externally, trade realignment, onshoring trends and slower global growth are making the operating environment more complex.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Internally, firms must navigate digitalisation, artificial intelligence (AI) adoption, workforce redesign and sustainability pressures.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But the key question is whether they are sufficiently deep to drive real transformation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How are our Industry Transformation Maps evolving to move firms up the value chain, rather than simply helping them manage costs?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How are we measuring genuine productivity gains, not just adoption of digital tools, but outcomes such as management upgrading, process redesign and business model transformation?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More fundamentally, how are we ensuring that firms build internal capabilities, in management, innovation and operations, that generate sustained productivity gains and diffuse across the wider economy?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More broadly, we should continue refining how our fiscal tools support transformation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, can we design more targeted AI diffusion support for small and medium enterprises (SMEs), tied to measurable outcomes such as productivity improvements, cost savings or new market access?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More broadly, our fiscal tools should be fast, targeted and where appropriate automatic, supporting adjustment while reinforcing long-term discipline.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While we focus on tradeable sectors, we must not neglect domestic sectors such as tourism, retail and food and beverage (F&B).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Could the Minister provide an update on the Tourism 2040 roadmap?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What are the key milestones for achieving "quality tourism"?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In an increasingly competitive region, with strong investments by neighbours such as Malaysia and Vietnam, how are we sharpening Singapore’s differentiation while managing the churn in attractions, restaurants and lifestyle offerings?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On the Greater Sentosa Master Plan, what progress can be made, and what is the projected economic contribution and job creation?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More broadly, are we developing precinct-level strategies, such as waterfront, cultural and lifestyle clusters, in a more coordinated way?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A vibrant domestic services sector is not just supportive.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It can itself be a source of innovation, productivity and capability development.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I agree that Singapore must stay ahead in advanced manufacturing, high-trust services and frontier domains, such as quantum, decarbonisation and space.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What are the projected job creation numbers over the next five to 10 years and how are these distributed across skill levels?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In advanced manufacturing, how are we ensuring that investments deepen local technical capabilities, not just raise output per worker?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In trust-based services, such as financial services, arbitration and digital trust, how are we sustaining Singapore’s advantage as global regulatory regimes evolve?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And in frontier sectors, what is the realistic timeline for scalable job creation?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It must build capabilities that endure and diffuse across the economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One key area is the transfer of capabilities from foreign talent to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How effective has the Capability Transfer Programme been in practice?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Where foreign expertise is required, are we embedding structured and measurable capability transfer requirements as part of investment conditions?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are firms receiving incentives required to demonstrate progression of Singaporeans into higher-value roles?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Sustainable growth must ultimately be driven by the accumulation of local human capital and knowledge.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the same time, skills supply must keep pace with demand.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is the Ministry working closely with our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) to anticipate manpower needs in priority sectors?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given the cross-Ministry nature of this effort, how is coordination being strengthened to ensure timely and aligned talent development?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Fifth, Mr Chairman, energy security and economic resilience.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a resource-scarce country, we must accelerate our transition to greener energy to reduce vulnerability to global price shocks, especially in an era of heightened geopolitical fragmentation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How does Singapore compare and how has our progress evolved over time?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, our economic environment is undergoing deep structural change, requiring bold and coordinated action rather than incremental adjustments.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Growth must translate into jobs for Singaporeans and openness without anchoring local capability is unsustainable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In a more volatile global environment, fiscal discipline and buffers give us the space to respond to shocks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But ultimately, our long-term competitiveness will depend on how deeply we build, retain and renew capabilities within our economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I look forward to MTI's clarifications on how it is sequencing these priorities and measuring success, not just in investment commitments, but in sustained capability development and meaningful employment outcomes for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Mr Chairman, before I begin, I declare my interest as the group managing director of Commonwealth Capital Group.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I have spoken in this House before about the importance of growing Singaporean multinational companies (MNCs) that are deeply rooted here.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: When a Singapore enterprise scales successfully, it anchors high value headquarter (HQ) functions here.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It develops local managerial talent pipelines, and it contributes to economic and supply chain resilience.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Singaporeans will benefit if we have more local companies crossing the $1 billion mark in annual revenues.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: While it remains important to help the broad base of small and medium enterprises (SMEs), as defined by those earning below $100 million of annual revenue, there are unique challenges for companies to scale beyond $100 million.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: At the $100 million-level, these companies are still small enterprises on the global stage.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, the support levels can drop from 70% to 30%.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I wonder if this is incentivising some companies to stay below the $100 million mark in annual revenues unnaturally.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: This is similar to legislation passing through the European parliament last week on a new tier of small mid-cap companies.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Coincidentally, this new tier was set at 200 million Euros.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Many of our larger local companies are already winners in their respective industries.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: They are capable and ambitious, yet few manage to break into the next tier.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: That is because unlike other countries, we do not have a large domestic market.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: So, to scale further, our firms have to internationalise when they are smaller while operating headquarters with a higher-cost base.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: This is a structural disadvantage and makes scaling much more difficult.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: So, to be clear, when the Government supports larger local firms to scale, it is no longer about picking future winners.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It is instead about doubling down on current winners, helping them win even bigger in the future and thereby bringing more benefits to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: First, firms must develop more products and services with market fit.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government has no business in telling companies what to do or how to do it.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: But the Government can create a conducive economic infrastructure to improve the chances of success.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: MTI's efforts to sustain a dynamic and vibrant enterprise ecosystem will help.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Such an ecosystem can foster broader, deeper and richer collaborations that lead to a faster cycle of product development and market testing.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We also need to consider whether our factors of production, taken holistically, are competitive.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: These include manpower, land, energy and capital, to name a few.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Firms need access to sufficiently affordable capital in order to invest in fixed assets, such as machines to increase output, as well as working capital, which can grow quite quickly as firms scale.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: To that end, I have no objections to the Budget announcement to improve the Enterprise Financing Scheme for trade and fixed asset loans.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We should be more impatient and help firms get to the moon faster.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Focus on inorganic growth through mergers and acquisitions (M&A) to turbocharge our local companies.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: This was not mentioned in the Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, once firms have product-market fit, they need to scale through new markets.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We can do this in a few ways.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We can bring those markets into Singapore through tourism.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: This speaks to our tourism strategy to bring more high-spending tourists who can revitalise traditionally domestic-oriented industries, like F&B and retail.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Of course, the more conventional way is to go into new markets overseas.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: When our firms expand overseas, the biggest constraints are often networks, credibility and distribution channels.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: This has traditionally been Government-led, but strong business-led communities can complement Government efforts.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: They can engage regulators and partners in a more informal and commercially driven manner; facilitate peer-to-peer sharing of intelligence and experiences; and build a sustained Singapore-branded presence.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I sometimes wonder why there are not more Singaporean business chambers of commerce overseas.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, there does not seem to be one in the United States (US) or the United Kingdom (UK).

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Is the Government aware of any coordination challenges preventing similar business-led platforms from forming?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Does the Government see any value in playing a stronger catalytic role to address these challenges?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Mr Chairman, I hope the Ministry can consider these perspectives to strengthen our enterprise landscape.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Singaporeans can look forward to a new generation of Singaporean global enterprises with pride.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Chairman, before I begin, I declare my interests as president of the Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE) as well as the co-chair of the Consumer Protection Review Panel.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I do appreciate CCS for taking enforcement action and securing injunctions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But when enforcement takes years, consumers continue to suffer losses while cases are being processed.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Errant businesses are allowed to continue their unfair practices for far too long.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, CCS already exercises administrative powers under the Competition Act.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I call on the Government to grant CCS similar administrative enforcement powers for breaches of the CPFTA.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Such powers would allow CCS to act more swiftly – to issue directions, require compliance and stop harmful practices without relying solely on lengthy Court proceedings.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This will free up judicial resources and, more importantly, protect our consumers earlier.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is especially critical as unfair practices evolve.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We are already seeing a rise in dark patterns – deceptive online design tactics that manipulate consumers into making unintended purchases.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These include hidden subscriptions, subscription traps that are difficult to cancel and AI-generated fake reviews that mislead consumers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Our enforcement tools must move just as quickly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A nimble digital economy requires a nimble regulator.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beyond digital practices, we are also deeply concerned about the sharp rise in prepayment losses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While many of these cases arise from certain sectors, the broader concern is this – businesses with weak financial standing continue to collect large prepayments to sustain cashflow.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Consumers should have time – away from sales pressure – to consider their purchases carefully and to reconsider large prepaid commitments.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It encourages responsible selling and gives consumers space to make rational decisions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Public consultations will begin on 16 March 2026.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I must stress that consumer protection is not anti-business.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Let us act decisively to protect that trust —

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Andre Low, you may take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chairman, let me begin with a Latin phrase every lawyer knows – caveat emptor.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This was a doctrine that was borne for a simpler world – a world of physical retail and handshakes, where buyer and sellers stood on more equal ground.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, the ordinary Singaporean faces sophisticated commercial machinery engineered to extract compliance in revenue through confusion, inertia and sometimes even fear.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The CPFTA was not designed for this world.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is falling short today and Singaporeans are paying the price.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will address two dimensions to this failure: first, the deceptive commercial practices that quietly train our wallets of everyday consumers; and second, the physical predation targeting our most vulnerable and destroying their retirement savings.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Long part of the playbook of usual suspects, like telecommunications companies (telcos) and gyms, the CCS has already demonstrated that such misconduct is spreading to other industries, like direct-to-consumer brands and e-commerce.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: COURTS knew about this in 2024 but they made no changes until the CCS intervened.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are just the headline cases, but beyond them, quieter practices extract money daily from consumers: fixed-term contracts advertised at introductory rates that apply only to the first few months, deliberately creating the impression that the full contract is cheaper than it really is; trials that convert silently to fully paid subscriptions with no active consent; and third-party services bundled into telco packages, like Netflix subscriptions, free for three months and then cancellable only by navigating a maze designed specifically to outlast the consumer's patience.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Each year, CASE and the CCS, between them, receive 40 to 50 complaints about such cases.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is just the tip of the iceberg and many similar tactics abound.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has convened a Consumer Protection Review Panel last March.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I welcome this and I look forward to its findings.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I also want to add my perspective about what I see as most urgent.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, any advertised price for fixed-term subscription must reflect the average cost across the full contract term.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A promotional rate that applies only part of the term cannot be used as the headline figure.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, we should ask for explicit active consent before any trial converts to a paid subscription.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If it is one click to sign up, it should be one click to cancel.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Four, we should empower the CCS with direct administrative powers like the UK's Competition and Markets Authority, which can levy fines of up to 10% of global annual revenue for consumer law breaches without going to Court.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, many companies behave well, but some bad actors act with impunity until they are taken to task.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to give the CCS stronger teeth to tackle their bad behaviour.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Voluntary compliance agreements after the fact are not deterrence.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Deceptive commercial practices drain wallets, but what I turn to now is worse – physical, face-to-face predatory behaviour that has cost some Singaporeans their retirement savings entirely.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Consider what happened at a hair salon chain, where an elderly man came in for an $8 haircut.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Midway through it, a staff member showed him images on a monitor and told him his scalp was haemorrhaging although no scanning device was ever used.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: His personal identification number (PIN) was entered into the payment machine while his payment total was covered.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He left having paid nearly $1,000 for treatments he never consented to.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another chain of beauty salons – 53 complaints, exceeding $980,000 in total.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In one case, a single consumer was charged at least $370,000.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More than 40% of complainants were aged 60 and above.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Its managing director was sentenced to four months' imprisonment in September 2024 – but note this – for contempt of Court, for failing to notify customers of injunctions against the chain, but not for the original predatory behaviour.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That was handled as a civil matter throughout.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The "abus de faiblesse", abuse of weakness crime, carries up to three years imprisonment for exploiting a consumer's age, illness or psychological vulnerability.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The UK's consumer protection legislation similarly expressly prohibits aggressive commercial practices, with penalties extending up to two years imprisonment.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chairman, when a business confines a vulnerable senior in a room, manufactures a medical scare and then extracts their life savings through coercion or psychological tactics, the law must have a name for that and consequences to match.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to declare that I have innovation studios which create and invest in technology and innovation ventures for the global market.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: We are actually living in a very exciting time, with lots of disruptive innovations and technology.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The question is how we in Singapore explore and exploit such opportunities.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: If we look at the, let us say, air taxi market that I am involved in, you can see that there are, on NASDAC or NYSE, companies that are worth between about $8 billion and $16 billion in valuations, but they have not sold a single craft.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: They have pre-orders, but they have not actually sold a single craft.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, they are pre-commercialisation, but the market recognise the opportunities and fund them.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Do we have such an exchange in Singapore?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: For technology companies and especially new ventures, really, we need to find a different formula.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: We can learn a little bit from that, but they cater for a bigger market.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, we have lots of startups, technology ventures resulting from the universities' research, and also from the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), from our research institutes.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: There are also a lot of AI innovation opportunities from the private sector.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The question is always a gap, the gap between the people that are looking for money and the people looking for exit from the investment.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, they are all staring at each other.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: That is where the pre-commercialisation stage funding is required for all these technology ventures.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: That for technology ventures that are globally oriented and leadership driven, g-o-l-d, I will call it these gold nuggets that we have.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And I believe we have a lot of gold nuggets.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I have trained a lot of innovative teams in the universities.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, how to bring these gold nuggets to become actually a big gold bar?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that our exchange can be structured for special listing rules for the technology ventures in the size of about $50 to $100 to 150 million, giving them the special access so that the —

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They provide economic stability for the nation and livelihoods for many workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They employ 45% of our workers but contribute only 11% of nominal value added.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These businesses can afford to pay their workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: ASME has observed that the current classification of SMEs is too broad.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A micro enterprise with 10 employees and $1 million in revenue, faces fundamentally different hurdles compared to a medium-sized company with 200 staff and $100 million in turnover.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By grouping them together, we risk applying one size fits all solutions that may not reach the smallest players.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Would the Government adopt ASME's suggestion to delineate micro enterprises and SMEs in national policy-making and data collection?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Tailoring grants and other assistance to the specific operational realities of each tier will make Government support more effective for them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Focusing more on these micro and small enterprises is a significant opportunity to lift the wages of many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to speak on SME transformation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In supporting transformation, we must recognise that many SMEs are family-run businesses facing generational succession and ownership transitions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Business transformation often cannot progress meaningfully until ownership structures are stabilised.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Where succession is unclear or governance frameworks remain informal, it becomes difficult to invest in digitalisation, expansion or strategic pivots.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I therefore suggest that our SME transformation framework integrate succession planning and family ownership transition as core components of enterprise upgrading.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Cultural nuances also shape how ethnic family businesses approach governance and decision-making.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This was evident during a Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) of Finance, Trade and Industry engagement with the Singapore Malay Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SMCCI), where heritage businesses shared how cultural norms influence succession and continuity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Different communities may view succession and professionalisation differently, and a one-size-fits-all model may not be effective.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Enterprise Singapore could deepen engagement with ethnic chambers such as the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SCCCI), the SMCCI, and the Singapore Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SICCI) to support more tailored approaches.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Institutions such as Singapore Management University’s Business Families Institute can partner with chambers to develop tailored succession playbooks.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As more heritage SMEs reach generational handover points, a smooth ownership transition is critical to preserving long-established enterprises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By integrating succession support into SME transformation policies, we can strengthen long-term enterprise resilience while retaining the cultural and social value that these businesses contribute to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If no Singaporean should be left behind, then I think no SME should be left behind too.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Much has been said about supporting individuals across different groups in the past few days.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: These are important sharing and decisions, yet, beyond assistance, many Singaporeans are asking fundamental questions.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Where are the good jobs and how do we secure them?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Singaporeans want opportunities and not depend on just Government handouts.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They ask not for a fish, but for the skill and an environment that can allow them to fish for themselves.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For that to happen, our SMEs must thrive.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When a company grows, workers grow with them.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Over the years, many schemes have been introduced to support SMEs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The issue today is often not about availability, but the ease of accessibility.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Many SME owners are fully occupied in their daily operations.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They do not have the bandwidth to navigate multiple schemes.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Firms with stronger administrative support navigate the system easier.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Smaller enterprises, often those who need the most help may not even know where to begin.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Perhaps the next step is to make the access to support the more proactive and intelligent.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Using secure login data, such a system could guide business owners in real time and outline the next step clearly.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This would simplify navigation and help ensure that no SME is left behind simply because it lacks time or administrative capability.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For a seed to grow into a healthy and strong tree, sunlight alone is never sufficient.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It needs fertile soil and a stable environment.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In our economics, we can imagine enterprises are the seeds and Singapore business environment is like the soil.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The rule of law, financial stability and open trade networks form the foundation for growth.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For example, the Economic Development Board (EDB) shapes the strategy direction.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Enterprise Singapore supports the upgrading and capability building.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) advances job redesign and skill upgrading so worker grows alongside with businesses.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This comes timely, yet businesses ask, are the processes clear?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For many SMEs, complexity itself becomes a barrier.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If the soil is stable, business will take root.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If the pathway is clear, they will grow.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: AI must deliver productivity and not just promise.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Enterprises care about outcomes, reducing administrative work, improving responsiveness and strengthening data management.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Our objective must reflect real productivity gains and not cost inflation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When strategy investments are brought into Singapore, are local enterprises supported to build capability at the same time?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When company upgrades system, can job redesign and skill upgrading move together?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If policies too, are better aligned, businesses will spend less time navigating schemes and more time transforming.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As our region accelerates transformation, Singapore must ensure that our SMEs are active participants and not bystanders.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Our task is to keep the soil fertile so that our enterprise, the seed of our economy can grow steadily and strongly.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: (In Mandarin):   SMEs are the foundation of the economy.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Enterprises are like seeds and the environment is like soil.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When enterprises are able to develop, the people benefit.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The key to policy lies in ensuring that supported projects and initiatives truly take root, work in synergy and operate efficiently.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If I could describe this in one sentence, it would be: "Strengthen enterprises to invigorate business; invigorate business to benefit the people." That is to say, when we strengthen enterprises, we also invigorate business, and when business is invigorated, the people will benefit.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, besides an income and wealth gap, I would like to explore a third gap, the enterprise ecosystem gap.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: A strong business ecosystem requires both MNC investments and a resilient SME base.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: They are two sides of the same coin.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: When MNCs grow, they bring capital and technology.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: But our SMEs must be able to grow alongside them and support them locally and regionally.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Today, many MNCs are incentivised to invest heavily in AI and robotics.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: While this strengthens our economy, it also accelerates disruption across supply chains.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: With the recent changes to our Preferential Additional Registration Fee rebates, let me use example of a car workshop.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: With EVs, there is no engine oil change and fewer mechanical components.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: These shifts recurring revenue patterns and affects the broader after-market value chain, from workshops to parts distributors.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, newer EVs require proprietary diagnostic software.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Independent workshops may lack authorised access or compatible systems.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This results in a technology and access issue.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: On the other hand, many workshops are not yet using AI tools for diagnostics, inventory planning or cash flow management.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This lowers the barrier to adoption and allows business owners to experiment, learn and integrate AI into daily operations before committing long term.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: As we push ahead with AI and advanced industry, we must ensure our SMEs are equipped to adapt alongside the industries we are transforming.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, on helping our SMEs grow and thrive.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We have advisory support, such as CTO-as-a-Service; intermediaries like the Singapore Business Federation, SME Centres and ASME; platforms like GoBusiness; the Productivity Solutions Grant and the Enterprise Development Grant, even AI Centres of Excellence.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: SMEs can be segmented by digital maturity and sector.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They can access advice on human resources, marketing, finance and operations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many SMEs are still struggling; not just to transform but to stay afloat.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Owners are consumed by rent, manpower, compliance and cashflow issues.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Diagnostics can identify gaps, but implementation requires managers who can redesign workflows, integrate systems, manage change and measure returns.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In F&B especially, margins are thin and volatility is high.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Entry barriers remain however relatively low, yet closure rates are high.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many enter without fully appreciating labour intensity, rental volatility and tight margins.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Even with grants, a fragile cost base makes transformation daunting.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Can we develop clearer readiness indicators, so that support is more disciplined and catalytic?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At the same time, how do we avoid leaving behind firms that require capability-building before they can qualify for deeper transformation support?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We have built platforms, provided grants and created segmentation tools.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I ask: do we need more precise industry segmentation, not just by size or digital maturity, but by structural conditions?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Are we investing enough in building internal execution capability and upgrading the capability of intermediaries who advise SMEs?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Can we introduce measures that free up leadership bandwidth for strategic upgrading?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the AI era, survival and superficial adoption are not enough.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, how will the Government help bridge this implementation gap, so that our SMEs can truly thrive?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Rental and manpower are among their largest cost components.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Compliance burden is also a concern, and I had raised this in my cut to MOF last week.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Beyond general labour shortages, firms increasingly need digitally skilled talent who can deploy AI to raise productivity, automate routine tasks and scale operations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: They also require coherent enterprise‑level AI strategies and rapid transformation to stay competitive in this AI era.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The measures in Budget 2026 are therefore welcome.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I just have one question on this particular point.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: On rentals, there had been speculations that foreign capital inflows are pushing up commercial rents and crowding out local operators.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Even though Chinese owners account for only 3% of retail businesses, the perception of displacement cannot be ignored, and this can affect community sentiment and our unique Singapore “personality”.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: What steps will MTI take to ensure local SMEs remain the anchor in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Will MTI expand programmes to help these SMEs further optimise costs in areas, such as group procurement, energy efficiency grants, shared services, market access and trade facilitation?

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, I would like to declare that I am the executive chairman of Enercon Asia, a company with presence in seven countries.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: In light of the tariffs imposed by the US on various countries, including Singapore, it is crucial for the Ministry to explore potential partnerships with other nations and develop additional Free Trade Agreements (FTAs).

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The importance of diversifying our business relationships cannot be overstated.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: It would be beneficial for the Ministries to provide guidance on which countries present valuable opportunities for our businesses to establish connections and a presence.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: As a small nation, Singapore must seek assistance and explore opportunities globally to thrive in the current economic landscape.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, first let me declare my interest as chief executive officer of an investment firm and advisor to companies investing in Singapore and other parts of the world.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During the Budget debate, I spoke about trust as Singapore’s competitive advantage in a fragmenting world.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to expand our economic space, to change from a GDP to a gross national product (GNP) mindset, linking up in a network with cities, their hinterlands and their peoples who are aligned with us.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, I propose four practical ways to shift towards becoming a networked economy.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Shift one, let us measure economic value created beyond our borders.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For decades, we measured GDP, activity within Singapore’s borders.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But over the years, more and more Singaporeans and firms operate and create value overseas.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Shift two: let us encourage Singaporean firms to hunt as a pack overseas.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A good place to start is the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (SEZ).

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should view the SEZ as an extra lung, where our SMEs can grow and thrive.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Suggestion one – position Singapore as the trusted gateway to the SEZ.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us take a proactive approach in marketing the Johor-Singapore SEZ.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As I shared in my Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) Committee of Supply (COS) cut, foreign policy can support our economic effort to expand our economic space as a networked economy.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to work closely, more closely, with our Malaysian counterparts.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This can deepen interdependence and create stronger ties for mutual benefit.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It will need a calibration of the mutual trust, given our past experience.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But the strategic direction is clear from the perspective of any inward foreign investor.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Johor and Singapore can and will play a synergistic role for them.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore anchors the trust-dependent core – headquarters governance, treasury, IP, data, compliance and legal, while the Johor hinterland provides scalable economic space.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The second suggestion – how can we organise a plug-and-play SME ecosystem?

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore's effort to bring inward investments into the SEZ should become business opportunities for our local SMEs.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To achieve this, we can structure a SEZ supplier programme where we, for instance, can identify the inward investors, input requirements and standards.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We pre-qualify SMEs who can meet such standards and finally, we match them to these anchors or inward investors.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Suggestion three – let us develop sectoral investment packages.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These can be identified in certain strategic industries, for example, manufacturing and logistics, digital and data services, food production and coaching, businesses that can take advantage of Johor's strength and Singapore's complementarities.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Each package can include shared infrastructure options, regulatory playbooks, talent and professional services support and a directory of Singapore SME suppliers.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: MTI can track outcomes, such as the number of two-side deployments across Singapore and the SEZ by sector.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We can look at the number of Singapore SMEs matched successfully with inward investors, and we can also measure incremental SME revenue as a result of using such complementarities across Johor and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And let me continue with shift three, creating good jobs overseas for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, there are young and mid-career Singaporeans who may not be aware of the opportunities in the region or some who are unable to price in the risk of working overseas.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, I suggest considering: one, curating overseas job placements for Singaporeans from entry to senior roles.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Two, we can offer incentives for firms to rotate staff regionally so that it becomes part of their career development.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Three, we can provide support and flexible childcare or education pathways for Singaporeans returning home.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Shift four: towards a network economy, developing artificial intelligence (AI) as our trusted Infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, regional ports are adopting AI independently.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Who provides the trusted platform where competing ports can share data for network optimisation?

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In cross-border finance, each financial institution is building its own AI infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But who can offer the coordination layer for these tools to work together so that capital can flow efficiently?

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By developing and leading effective AI governance and secure data exchange frameworks.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In a fragmented world, the trusted coordinator becomes invaluable.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In closing, Mr Chairman, MTI, MFA, the Ministry of Manpower and our economic agencies are doing a fine job.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Chairman, over the past 30 years, many MNCs have based their Asia Pacific headquarters in Singapore, positioning us as a gateway for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In a volatile global environment, economic connection is more critical than ever.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Regional collaboration with ASEAN, including initiatives, like the Johor-Singapore SEZ, has unlocked competitive and strategic advantages for all parties.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many businesses and workers lack experience operating beyond Singapore.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Schemes, like the Enterprise Development Grant, help defray the costs of setting up businesses abroad.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will MTI consider strengthening such support to provide smoother, lower-risk entry into foreign markets?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On the manpower front, will MTI expand the Global Ready Talent Programme or explore grants to co-fund Singaporeans' relocation costs within ASEAN?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If not, can MTI share how it plans to build capacity in three areas: first, increasing international firms' readiness to appoint Singaporeans to regional roles; second, strengthening business leaders' ability to operate in diverse markets; and third, encouraging Singaporeans to relocate for regional opportunities?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If Singapore is to remain a gateway to ASEAN, we must not only host regional headquarters, we must raise a generation of Singaporeans ready to lead beyond our shores.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, in a tighter Singapore, domestic scale alone will not sustain enterprise growth.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For Singapore businesses, internationalisation is essential for long-term competitiveness and resilience.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Middle East conflict that unfolded over the weekend reflects how quickly geopolitical conditions can shift.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Energy markets react, insurance premiums adjust, shipping routes are reassessed and payment and compliance risks increase.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In such an environment, uncertainty can cause firms to hesitate.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: How will MTI continue to send a strong and consistent message that despite heightened geopolitical risks, Singapore firms must press on with internationalisation and that the Government will stand behind them as they do so?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, we must recognise internationalisation risk is not uniform.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Parts of Southeast Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Latin America often carry elevated political, regulatory and receivable risks.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Second, many overseas projects today are too large or too complex for individual SMEs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Procurement frameworks favour scale, track record and integrated capability.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Could existing schemes be restructured more explicitly to support consortium-based international bids, including shared financing and coordinated market entry?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We must strengthen not just financing support, but market intelligence, corridor expertise and in-market execution platforms.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In a more uncertain world, the answer is not retreat.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is a calibrated expansion backed by credible risk-sharing and a confident ecosystem —

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2026 positions AI, alongside strategic capabilities such as quantum, advanced manufacturing and space, as critical to Singapore's ability to thrive in a changed world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: The thrust is clear – upgrade firms, reskill workers and build new growth engines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: But transformation will not be fully realised without our entrepreneurs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Technological shifts do not only upgrade incumbents, they create new markets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Advanced manufacturing and deep tech open new value chains.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: As we build capabilities within firms, we must also enable more Singaporeans to build new ventures around these emerging domains.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: About half of new firms do not survive beyond five years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: When people see these statistics, the instinctive response is, "It's too risky.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: We don't want to try." But if too few are willing to try, the economy suffers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: To bridge that gap, we must reduce the perception that entrepreneurship carries a permanent career penalty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Entrepreneurship should be normalised as another step in a career journey, not a make-or-break endpoint.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: It should be seen as part of lifelong learning – a period of experimentation, skill development and value creation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: After all, research shows that the average founder of high-growth firms are in their early to mid-40s.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Experience and networks matter, especially in complex sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Small nations, like ours, cannot afford permanent talent loss from temporary setbacks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Second, we can convert national missions into startup growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: As sectoral missions unlock opportunities in AI, manufacturing, connectivity and healthcare, how do we ensure Singapore-based startups are meaningfully plugged into these platforms?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Can procurement pathways, pilot projects and structured partnerships be strengthened so that startups led by Singapore-based founders can validate and scale?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: In frontier sectors, such as quantum and space, can cross-agency sandbox models support experimentation and co-learning while accelerating deployment?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: If we get this right, national missions can catalyse local venture growth and not just enterprise upgrading.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: It is one thing to grow new ventures here, it is quite another to ensure that as they scale globally, they remain anchored in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: If strategic decision-making, IP and leadership functions relocate elsewhere in pursuit of capital and customers, we risk losing gains in control, capital formation and ecosystem spillovers.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan
text: Chairman, I would like to speak on three things: funding, founders and talent for our startups.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan
text: Is the constraint today early-stage formation or is it at the growth stage, where companies have product-market fit but struggle to scale regionally?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan
text: Is it a shortage of later-stage capital or is it a lack of sector depth in areas, such as deep tech and industrial solutions?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan
text: I would appreciate clarity on how MTI has diagnosed this gap and how the capital will be deployed?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan
text: Are we crowding in experienced regional and global growth funds?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan
text: Are we co-investing alongside operators who can help companies to expand beyond Singapore?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan
text: We should also avoid concentrating public funds within the same small pool of startups.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan
text: Co-investment should widen participation, deepen sector capabilities and bring in new founders and new markets.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan
text: But we know that startups fail due to a myriad of reasons.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan
text: In the spirit of supporting and encouraging entrepreneurship, I would like to check if this criterion can be reviewed?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan
text: On talents, hiring a full-time chief AI officer can be costly for early-stage firms.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan
text: This is distinct from the chief technology officer (CTO) advisory schemes.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan
text: A chief AI officer shapes data strategy, model development and responsible AI use across the organisation.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan
text: Funding, talents and founders help companies to grow.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Chairman, let me thank all Members who have spoken on MTI's COS.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: At the same time, we must be clear-eyed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Singapore is entering a new phase in our economic journey.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The rules that allowed Singapore to prosper for decades have fundamentally changed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We face a more complex global environment, marked by heightened great-power competition, rising protectionism and a more fragmented global order.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: President Trump has also announced that he intends to raise it to 15%.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There is still considerable uncertainty about how the tariff will evolve over time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are working with the Singapore Economic Resilience Taskforce (SERT) tripartite members to provide information to and gather feedback from businesses and workers to help them navigate these uncertainties.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These developments exemplify the unpredictable and uncertain global trading environment that we must now navigate.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Over the weekend, the conflict in the Middle East escalated, with the US and Israel launching an attack on Iran, and Iran retaliating by counterattacking Israel and US' bases in the region.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In the near term, this could result in an increase in global energy prices.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Depending on how protracted the conflict is, higher energy prices could lead to higher costs for businesses and consumers and weigh on the global and Singapore economies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are monitoring the developments closely and will reassess our GDP and inflation forecasts if necessary.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Major structural forces are also reshaping industries, businesses and jobs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: AI and automation are transforming how value is created and how work is organised.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The global push to decarbonisation is also changing industrial processes, influencing investment patterns and impacting relative competitiveness.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Together with our demographic constraints that I spoke about last week, sustaining growth and creating good jobs will become more challenging.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Yet even in this more difficult environment, there are good opportunities for Singapore as a trusted, knowledge-driven and connected hub.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: First, we will establish and deepen our leadership in key growth sectors, while pushing the frontier into new areas of growth.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As our economy matures, growth and good jobs can no longer come from scale alone.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Growth must increasingly come from depth – by establishing and deepening global leadership in sectors where Singapore already has strong foundations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about our plans for the advanced manufacturing, trust-based services and frontier sectors.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Singapore is already a global node in advanced manufacturing sectors, such as semiconductors, medical products, specialty chemicals and aerospace, which contribute significantly to our economy and provide good jobs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We want to secure and extend our leadership in these sectors – we will step up investments in AI, automation and digital technologies to raise productivity, improve quality and reliability, and become more flexible and resilient.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As factories become more automated and data-driven, demand will grow for skilled jobs, such as automation and robotics engineers, process engineers, data specialists and advanced equipment technicians, that command higher wages.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will also focus research and development (R&D) resources to sharpen our technological edge, shorten innovation cycles and help firms move ideas faster – from the lab to the factory floor and into the market.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In parallel, we will accelerate the adoption of low-carbon and resource-efficient technologies, so that our industries remain competitive as the world transitions to a low-carbon future.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: By reinforcing these strengths, we will build deep, competitive ecosystems that anchor high-value activities here and support good, skilled jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Beyond manufacturing, we are also extending our lead in modern services.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In this volatile and uncertain world, trust has become the most sought-after asset.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our trust premium has enabled us to establish ourselves as a global hub for finance, capital and IP.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will build on this to develop Singapore as a global hub for trust-based services, such as risk advisory, cybersecurity, AI assurance and Testing, Inspection and Certification.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will create new opportunities in modern services.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Even as we deepen our existing strengths in advanced manufacturing and modern services, we must also push the frontier into new areas of growth, such as quantum, decarbonisation technologies and space-related industries.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As these industries grow, they will open up new career opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Taken together, these will deepen what we already do well in advanced manufacturing and modern services, while creating new engines and expand Singapore's growth frontier, and secure high-quality jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Second, we must sustain a dynamic and vibrant enterprise ecosystem, spanning multinational corporations, high-growth companies and a vibrant start-up community.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Leading MNCs, both local and foreign, will continue to be a core pillar of our economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: They bring scale, advanced technologies, global networks and high-quality jobs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will continue to work with MNCs to anchor high-value activities here, including R&D, advanced manufacturing, regional and global headquarters functions, and strategic roles.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: At the same time, the next phase of growth will increasingly come from a new generation of emerging enterprises – growth-stage companies that have yet to establish themselves as a leading MNC but have demonstrated both the potential and ambition to become future industry leaders.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We must be prepared to take some risks to support such promising enterprises by providing them with a trusted base to operate from, and scale to international markets.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: One such company is Workato, an enterprise software firm that helps businesses automate workflows and integrate systems across their operations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Singapore can serve as a strategic base for Workato's global expansion, anchoring product development, AI innovation and regional leadership here, while creating high-value opportunities for Singaporeans and strengthening our talent pipeline.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I agree with Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh that anchoring and partnering companies, like Workato, in Singapore at an early stage of their growth is important as it would allow us to shape where strategic HQ decisions are made, where core capabilities are built and where long-term value is created.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As these companies grow from Singapore, they will create new roles here in areas, such as R&D, product management, marketing and business development.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: EDB will step up efforts to identify and anchor such companies, working closely with leading venture capital and private equity partners.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will provide bespoke, end-to-end support, such as market access assistance, regulatory facilitation and access to ready-to-use facilities, to help these companies anchor in Singapore and grow their presence here.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Done well, this will allow us to capture long-term economic value, strengthen our pipeline of leading enterprises and reinforce Singapore's position as a trusted base for globally leading companies to be here and to scale.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will not just be a landing pad, but also a launching pad for potential global companies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Alongside this, we will continue to sustain the vibrancy of our start-up community and foster an entrepreneurial culture where people dare to dream and take risks.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Minister of State Alvin Tan will share more on our plans for our startups.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: By sustaining dynamic and vibrant enterprise ecosystems, we will reinforce Singapore's position as a trusted and connected base for global business and ensure that our economy remains at the forefront of innovation and growth.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For our enterprises to raise productivity, upgrade capabilities and scale innovation faster than before, AI is the critical enabler.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our third thrust is therefore to establish Singapore as an AI leader, as well as an AI-empowered economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We want to empower our companies to harness AI end-to-end, by redesigning business processes, embedding AI into core operations, developing proprietary applications, transforming workflows and upgrading jobs and skills.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Under this programme, we will target a select group of Singapore-based companies with the ambition and commitment to make AI a core driver of productivity, innovation and growth.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will partner these companies to transform their businesses, by embedding AI across core operations, organisational processes and workforce practices.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This includes leadership and workforce training, as well as support to develop and execute AI transformation projects with clear and measurable business impact.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These companies will also invest in retraining and upskilling their employees, enabling their workers to take on high-value AI-enabled job roles.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: AI has been embedded throughout the bank's operations, from customer engagement to risk management and operational efficiency.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For instance, through personalised AI-driven nudges, DBS guides retail customers to make better investment and financial decisions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These customers saved twice as much, invested five times more and had nearly three times higher insurance coverage than those who did not.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In risk management, AI analyses millions of transactions daily to detect unusual patterns and intercept suspicious activity in real-time to better protect its customers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This helps businesses move faster, with greater certainty, especially in cross-border transactions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: DBS is equipping all 40,000 of its employees with foundational understanding and practical exposure to AI.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It is also reskilling employees into new job roles that are being created through the integration of AI – for example, from customer service officers into AI agent monitoring managers and GenAI evaluators.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: AI has also provided some employees with the opportunity to move into new career pathways – for instance, from customer service roles into relationship management roles.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: DBS' journey demonstrates how companies can deploy AI to enhance business value while strengthening their workforce.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will learn from their experiences, show the way forward and give other firms the confidence to move faster and deeper in their own AI journeys.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For each Mission, we will work with the industry to define sharp, sector-specific problem statements in areas where AI can drive breakthrough transformations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Around each Mission, we will build full-stack ecosystems, including datasets, computing resources, regulatory sandboxes and solution providers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will shorten the path from development to deployment and from testing to scale.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These Missions will generate demand for new skills, creating clusters of expertise anchored in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: AI Missions serve as rallying flags to attract global AI talent and companies focused on real-world applications, mobilise whole-of-nation efforts across the Government and industry, and concentrate investments and enablers for greater impact.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These efforts – "Champions of AI", AI Missions and "Kampong AI" – will position Singapore as a place where AI solutions are built, proven and scaled, empowering firms across the economy and establishing AI leadership in key sectors.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Even as we grow our economy, our competitiveness will depend not only on innovation, but also on the ability of our businesses to adapt, reposition and transform.
