text: Countries are prioritising economic security over open markets and competition for investments is intensifying.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Mr Azhar Othman asked how we could better support our firms to access overseas markets.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: In this uncertain environment, strong international partnerships are more crucial than ever to help our firms internationalise.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: First, we are deepening our economic ties with key partners.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We continue to engage with the US and China as long-standing partners based on shared economic interests.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We mark 60 years of Singapore-US diplomatic relations this year and we are expanding cooperation in AI, quantum and advanced nuclear energy technologies.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: With China, we continue to strengthen our economic partnership through flagship joint projects in Suzhou, Tianjin and Chongqing, which celebrated its 10th anniversary last year.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Meanwhile, we are enhancing our partnerships with other major economies.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We are deepening our engagements with India in high-value growth areas, such as semiconductors, aviation maintenance, repair and overhaul services and space technology, positioning Singapore companies as early movers into India's market.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: These will provide our companies with legal certainty in cross-regional digital transactions.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Closer to home, we continue to push for deeper regional economic integration through ASEAN.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: As Singapore assumes ASEAN Chairmanship next year, we will work with fellow members to build a more seamless economic community and accelerate growth in our digital and green economies.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We are diversifying our economic links with emerging markets and growth sectors to unlock new opportunities for Singapore firms.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We continue to work with our Latin American partners through FTAs with the Pacific Alliance and MERCOSUR, whilst venturing into South Asia, the Middle East and Africa with newer trade and investment agreements.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This will boost our firms' confidence to invest across these dynamic markets.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We have also launched negotiations on the Green Economy Partnership Agreement with Chile and New Zealand.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This is to keep our trade in essential goods, like food and pharmaceuticals, uninterrupted even during global crises.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We are partnering with like-minded countries to uphold and shape the open, rules-based multilateral trading system.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We launched the Future of Trade and Investment Partnership, bringing together 16 small, medium and trade-dependent countries to address emerging challenges and opportunities in global trade and investment.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We continue to expand high-quality regional agreements, like the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership and Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, while building bridges through inaugural dialogues between the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, EU and ASEAN.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Mr Chairman, our efforts to expand our economic space and create quality industrial spaces enable Singapore to remain a competitive destination for firms and to catalyse innovation.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: My MTI colleagues and I have shared on our strategies to create growth and good jobs for Singaporeans, and this is crucial amidst a climate of uncertainties.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We will strive to ensure that Singapore remains a trusted and dynamic hub for trade and capital, securing a brighter future for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: One is, on hearing Deputy Prime Minister's comments earlier from his speech, I would like to thank Deputy Prime Minister Gan for his quite extensive speech earlier.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: He mentioned about the reassessment of GDP and inflation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: First, is the scenario of potential tariff increases on key sectors, such as semiconductor and pharmaceuticals, that is one.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Second is, slowdown in global AI investment flows, if that happens.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Thirdly, Deputy Prime Minister mentioned just now about the protracted scenario of Middle East crisis and/or price shocks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The last question is to Minister of State Alvin Tan, I would like to thank him for his updates on the Greater Sentosa Master Plan in my cut.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As you have seen, the tariffs have been shifted from one legislation to another under the US.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And also, we have to take into account the reactions from the various countries in response to these tariffs, which have an impact on us.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Sometimes, when the tariffs go up, it slows down the economy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: When tariffs come down, it stimulates the economy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And as a result of tariffs going up, some economies may decide to front-load their exports, so they ramp up their manufacturing, they ramp up their exports and as a result of them ramping up their exports, they may then import more components from Singapore, and we supply components to them.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, it is a very complicated web of trading arrangements among countries, and we depend on a rules-based, open trading system.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, we really will benefit from the global economic growth.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If global tariffs are lower, then it will stimulate more economic activities and trade will flourish, and Singapore will benefit from it.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For tariffs, from Singapore's point of view, a lower tariff is better for us, because then it facilitates freer and more open trading activities, and that will benefit open economies, like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I think this is something that we always have to plan for.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have to continue to develop our trading network and we want to strengthen our resilience in our trading arrangement.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: That is why we continue to negotiate trading agreements in different forms, including digital agreements.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, that is how we strengthen our resilience in terms of our defence against the tariffs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: On investment in AI, this is something that we are embarking on and we hope to be able to attract both talent and investments, as well as solution providers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: They are able to come to Singapore and create this ecosystem among AI operators, AI stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: That is why we are now expanding our Lorong AI into a Kampong AI, so we have a bigger capacity, and we can bring together both working and living environment so that it is an entire ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And hopefully this will generate a momentum on its own and continue to attract more investments into AI.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: On the Middle East crisis, this just happened over the weekend.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And therefore, it is important as a supply channel for the world's energy needs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Singapore also depends significantly on supplies from the Middle East, in addition to our supplies in this region.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, it is something that we will continue to assess.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We do expect that if the conflict in the Middle East is protracted, I think it will have a significant impact on the overall energy cost.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Singapore over the last few years, as Minister Tan has explained, has built up our resilience.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have built in as several measures to strengthen our resilience against potential external shocks in energy supply.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Some of these we will not be able to share because they are confidential and security related, some of it I think Minister Tan has explained earlier.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I will ask him to elaborate if necessary.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: On the development expenditure, I will leave Minister Tan to talk about the energy expenditure for development.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But our development expenditure has a significant increase partly, because of the need to continue to attract investments.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As many of you are aware, with the introduction of the minimum tax, tax incentive is now less effective and therefore, we will need to look at other ways of anchoring key investments into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And this development expenditure is part of it.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is designated to allow us to be able to attract investments to come to Singapore to continue to provide good jobs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I will hand it over to Dr Tan.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And I also alluded to the SPEED office that is going to drive quite a number of these.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There are also requirements for us to start to embark on the greening of Jurong Island.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Separate to that, if you recall, either at last year's COS or the COS of the year before, Members of this House have also set aside a Future Energy Fund.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But that will be more related to infrastructure development, funding infrastructure for interconnectors to prepare them for some of the renewable energy imports.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do not have an exact breakdown as to which are the components.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There are sandboxes that we will need the incremental budget to develop, but each one of these pathways, as I have said, as we leave no stone unturned, we want to evaluate which can give us that sustainability, the reliability and also the security that is needed.

speaker: The Chairman
text: There is something for Minister of State Tan to respond to.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Chairman, I thank Mr Saktiandi Supaat for his interest in Sentosa.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And this is our key strategy: to attract high quality tourism.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: With all of the different phases that we will be building across the years, many new theme parks and also attractions, I think Sentosa will transform.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We welcome Singaporeans and visitors to visit and add to our tourism vibrancy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Chairman, I understand the Member's interest in the commercialisation of publicly funded research and also the returns on investments.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I share the same sentiment and passion as his interests.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Government is not investing in R&D like a commercial outfit alone.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It has to do significantly more than that.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It has to invest in R&D, to build over the longer term our strategic capabilities, the strategic capabilities that is required for our country, to continue to not just thrive, but to be able to run ahead of our competition.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And we are actually seeing fruits of our labour.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, the R&D capacity of our firms and our economy, it has increased significantly.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This has allowed our Singapore economy to move up the value chain of industries and activities and take global leadership positions in technologically-intensive sectors and, of course, in the process, creating good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The number of private sector R&D firms has also grown by 33% to 1,030 firms, from 2016 to 2023.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And over the same period, value-added contributed by R&D firms grew by 142%, and value-added per worker for R&D firms grew by 110%.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We take Mirxes, for example, which is one of the R&D firms nurtured by our ecosystem.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, 60% of its global staff are based here in Singapore and they are largely Singaporeans or Singapore PRs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is despite its listing in Hong Kong.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The increase in the R&D capacity has also enabled Singapore to establish leadership in technologically intensive sectors, such as semiconductors and biomedical and we could pursue frontier areas, such as space technology.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And today, Singapore is the sixth largest exporter of high-tech goods globally, according to the World Bank group.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Singapore has established itself as a leading global hub for biopharmaceutical manufacturing, with industry output doubling over the past two decades to exceed $18 billion in 2023.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And major pharmaceutical companies like Eli Lilly, MSD and Pfizer, continue to maintain R&D activities across precincts at One-North and Tuas Medical Park.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This strengthens our innovation-driven economy and positions Singapore at the forefront of emerging technologies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As Minister of State Alvin Tan mentioned earlier, our startup ecosystem is ranked fourth in the world in StartupBlink's Global Startup Ecosystem Index 2025.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Since 2020, Singapore's ranking as a startup ecosystem has climbed from 16th to fourth position and over the past five years, our tech startups have secured US$1 billion or more annually in venture capital investments.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Third, we have developed globally leading universities right at our doorstep for our Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: NUS and NTU, they were ranked eighth and 12th respectively in the QS World University Rankings in 2026.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Strong university rankings attract investments, drive innovation and it provide our own people with world-class education.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Riding on our strength in cultivating an adaptable, digitally fluent and innovation-ready workforce in the age of AI, Singapore was ranked first amongst 135 economies in the Overall Talent Competitiveness Index, based on 2025 Global Talent Competitiveness Index, overtaking Switzerland to the top spot.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: From 2014 to 2024, Singapore's Field-Weighted Citation Impact has risen from 1.44 to 1.76.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This means that our research is cited 76% more than the global average.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This reflects the high quality of our academic researchers and their work.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And fourth, our R&D capabilities also contributed significantly to our strategic priorities in areas such as healthcare, climate change and urban solutions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Not too long ago, during COVID-19, it was our researchers, who were amongst the first in the world to culture the SARS-CoV-2 virus.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They rapidly developed the diagnostic kits, and enabled data-driven public health measures.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I want to assure our hon Member, Mr Mark Lee, and all Members that we have generated good commercial traction from the scientific base that we have built over the past many decades.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These spin-offs range from MetaOptics, which leveraged on A*STAR's material and wafer fab expertise to make world class lenses and achieved a successful initial public offering (IPO); to Amperesand, which leveraged on NTU's advanced solid state transformer technology to extend its lead as a category leader.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Most of the information by the way that I have shared, can be found in public sources, such as the National Survey of RIE and our A*STAR annual report.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will always stay the course and we will continue to always invest in our future.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Next clarification, Mr Victor Lye, reward for your eight-minute cut.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye
text: Chairman, I thank the political officeholders for their response and speeches.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye
text: With regard to our investments in the advanced industries, the SMEs are going to have to transition, and I welcome Minister of State Gan Siow Huang's sharing about Woodlands Gateway.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye
text: My first question is, do we have any plans to perhaps develop an industrial estate, a Singapore industrial estate across from Singapore, so that we can deploy these two sites' gateway to the SEZ, which expands Singapore's economic space.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye
text: My second question is with regard to that, there is going to be a need for skilled labour.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye
text: Can we facilitate a framework whereby Singapore skilled workers can live and work in the SEZ?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Minister of State Gan, I hope your response will be shorter than Minister Tan's.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Chairman, I would like to ask the Minster Tan.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I am glad to hear that there are plans to see how we can utilise more of the alternative sources for energy, hydrogen being one of them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: So, I would like to understand whether Singapore is looking at positioning ourselves early, to shape the regional hydrogen energy supply chain instead of just following others, but to take the lead in this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: And also, as we look at overall energy, security and sustainability, what might be in place to support firms and startups, whether locally in Singapore, or to attract them to Singapore, to deepen their R&D in this area, and eventually towards commercialising the deployment of such energy, especially hydrogen, so that we can move towards that secure, sustainable and hopefully, affordable energy vision.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Last clarification is that we talk about affordability.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: As we digitalise, as we double down on the AI, consumption will definitely increase and also, as we import more of these energy into Singapore, there could be cost associated with this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: How do we mitigate or prevent such cost being passed on to local businesses and Singaporeans households so that it remains highly accessible and affordable to them?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Chairman, with your permission – because there are three clarification statements – I would try my best to be succinct and brief.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is just that today, the transportation of green hydrogen is very, very, very expensive and logistically, today, the chains are not established yet.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, as an intermediary, we will need a carrier and to carry that green hydrogen across, we carry it in the form of green ammonia.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we are working closely with the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore because our aspirations are beyond the FEED study, beyond the sandbox.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are hoping that eventually, we could potentially, if we are able to prove the viability and feasibility of that sandbox, we can, not just use that as one form of energy as part of our green hydrogen strategy, but we could also potentially be a bunkering hub in the transportation and the movement of green ammonia from the east to the west.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the second part, in terms of how we want to help the SMEs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To the third point on renewable energy imports.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Indeed, part of that diversification and energy transition resulting in lower carbon alternatives will come with costs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, the likes of, whether it is Google, Amazon Web Services, some of these data centres, we allow them to negotiate and we ring-fence it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But there will come a time when the Government will work with all of the different sectors alongside with our carbon tax to smear that price along.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It will not happen within this very short period of time, but it is also something that we have to take into consideration.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And with that, we hope to be able to socialise it across our entire population, our country.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The underlying principle has to be how we deal with, first and foremost, through energy conservation and how do we become a lot more efficient in managing peak pricing versus trial pricing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are also working on different simulated scenarios.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are also using energy storage systems to ensure that base load is always maintained.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think these are the paths that we will all have to undertake collectively as we move forward.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And of course, I look forward to the strong support of Ms Tin and fellow Members of this House as we decarbonise.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang
text: First, I want to thank Senior Minister of State Low for sharing what they are going to do for SMEs, in particular, from availability to making it easier to access in future.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang
text: But I thought I just wanted to ask this supplementary question in Mandarin, as it is more for the Chinese-speaking SMEs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang
text: (In Mandarin):   When adopting artificial intelligence, will the Government consider whether AI could be more automated, capable of translating into Chinese or other languages, as well as providing voice reading, so that Chinese-educated entrepreneurs can better understand and benefit more?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Please allow me to reply very succinctly to Mr Lee Hong Chuang, also in Mandarin.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: (In Mandarin):   I would like to thank Mr Lee Hong Chuang for his constructive question just now.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: When he was speaking in Chinese earlier, I was listening attentively.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: There was one sentence that I thought was very apt – that when enterprises do well, people have the greatest job security.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I think this is a very important social environment in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: MTI's English speeches earlier mentioned why we are vigorously launching the enterprise transformation package, which has three important components.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: First, we will vigorously promote our enterprises' adoption of AI technology.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Anyone who has visited China would have seen the technology Mr Lee mentioned; it is everywhere now.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: When we give speeches, Chinese, English or other languages are simultaneiously shown on the screen.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, we will definitely consider this constructive suggestion.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We also encourage enterprises to adopt not only AI, but also automation and energy-saving solutions, as Minister Tan See Leng mentioned earlier.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Second, I would like to make an appeal.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: MTI and Enterprise Singapore will definitely support our enterprises in developing not only the important local market, but also overseas markets.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I am actually using up all our break time in order to meet the guillotine time.

text: The guillotine time is 3.20 pm, so there will be no breaks this afternoon.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I will try to accommodate as much as possible, so, I suggest skip all the preambles, just ask your clarifications.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Likewise for the front benchers, skip all the — skip whatever you can, and just answer.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: The Deputy Prime Minister mentioned about how growth comes from depth and not just skill anymore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: And in a particular part, he said about shortening innovation cycles, and I presume it is about research translation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: And I think that is something Singapore is already doing.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: So, I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister, how are we doing it differently and are there specific targets in terms of the speed of research translation to shorten innovation cycle?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Also about the Business Refresh scheme that Senior Minister of State Low mentioned, I just wanted to check: are we expanding the scheme to also support business families with generational succession and pivot?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: And then second, what is the role of trade associations in helping to diffuse the benefits of the Business Refresh scheme?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: And in my experience working with trade associations, quite a distinct part of the success factor is also the secretariat.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: So, is MTI also supporting trade associations to beef up the capacity and capability of the secretariats?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These are the areas that we already have a strength.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We want to not just be one of the operators in the world, but we want to become a key node.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And by doing so, we also want to attract key operation functions here, including R&D.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, instead of doing R&D elsewhere, we want to encourage them to bring the R&D facilities here, build the R&D capabilities in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This will then help them shorten the process of bringing innovation to the market.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, I think this is one way that we are doing so.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Dr Tan has also mentioned about our initiatives in R&D, our investments in R&D and the translational research to facilitate the translation of knowledge into commercial products and services.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, these are the various efforts we are doing.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are also using AI to help us to see how we can facilitate and speed up the process of innovation.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, I think many companies are already introducing AI capabilities in the R&D process to allow them to do so.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I just want to make a very quick response to Mr Saktiandi Supaat's question earlier.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I think he asked what are the triggers for the Government to start to respond to many of these scenarios.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I just want to say that there is no single trigger.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will need to take into account holistically all the impact and make assessments as we go along.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As and when, if necessary, we will roll out initiatives to respond to these scenarios.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Under SERT, for example, we rolled out the Business Adaptation Grant (BizAdapt) and also rolled out GRIT as an internship programme to help support workers to do the transition.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, I think, as we go along, we will make assessments.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As and when necessary, we will roll out new initiatives to support businesses in this transition.
